name: POEMS syndrome
aliases: polyneuropathy organomegaly endocrinopathy M-protein skin changes

clinicalPearls: Rare paraneoplastic disorder driven by an underlying clonal plasma cell process, almost always with lambda light-chain restriction.
Peripheral polyneuropathy is typically the presenting and most disabling feature — usually a symmetric, ascending, demyelinating sensorimotor pattern resembling CIDP.
Suspect POEMS when 'CIDP' fails to respond to standard immunotherapy, especially if accompanied by systemic features.
Sclerotic bone lesions (solitary or multiple) are common and often visible on skeletal survey or CT even without lytic disease typical of myeloma.
Papilledema, extravascular volume overload (ascites, edema, effusions), and thrombocytosis/erythrocytosis are distinctive clues that separate POEMS from typical myeloma or CIDP.
Markedly elevated serum VEGF is a hallmark biomarker reflecting disease activity.
Endocrinopathies (commonly hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, or glucose intolerance) are frequent but nonspecific, and should not be over-interpreted alone.
Skin changes (hyperpigmentation, thickening, hypertrichosis, glomeruloid hemangiomas) support the diagnosis when present alongside neuropathy.
reference.pathophysiology: POEMS syndrome arises from an underlying monoclonal, lambda-restricted plasma cell disorder that drives systemic overproduction of proinflammatory and proangiogenic cytokines, most notably vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). This cytokine excess is thought to underlie the vascular, neurologic, and organ-based manifestations rather than direct tumor infiltration, distinguishing the disease from classic multiple myeloma. The resulting syndrome combines a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy with multisystem involvement including bone, endocrine, dermatologic, and extravascular fluid abnormalities.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) without associated plasma cell disorder
Castleman disease (may overlap with or occur alongside POEMS)
Diabetic or other systemic causes of sensorimotor polyneuropathy
nonInfectiousMimics: Diabetic polyneuropathy with unrelated monoclonal gammopathy (MGUS)
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — detects and characterizes the monoclonal (typically lambda) protein
Serum free light chain ratio — supports clonality assessment
Serum VEGF level — supports diagnosis and can track disease activity
Skeletal survey and/or whole-body imaging (CT or PET) — identifies characteristic sclerotic or mixed bone lesions
Nerve conduction studies/EMG — confirms demyelinating polyneuropathy pattern
Bone marrow biopsy — quantifies clonal plasma cells and excludes overt myeloma
Endocrine panel (thyroid, gonadal, adrenal, glucose) — screens for associated endocrinopathies
Echocardiography and pulmonary function testing — assesses for pulmonary hypertension and extravascular volume overload
redFlags: Rapidly progressive neuropathy with respiratory or bulbar involvement
New papilledema suggesting raised intracranial pressure
Signs of extravascular volume overload (ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema) indicating advancing systemic disease
Evidence of pulmonary hypertension or thrombotic events, which portend higher morbidity
Rapid rise in serum VEGF or new osteolytic transformation suggesting progression or evolution toward myeloma
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as idiopathic CIDP and treating with standard immunotherapy (e.g., IVIG/plasma exchange) alone, which is typically ineffective since the underlying plasma cell clone is not addressed
Overlooking sclerotic bone lesions on imaging because they lack the classic lytic appearance of multiple myeloma
Failing to check serum VEGF or overinterpreting an isolated endocrinopathy without considering the full multisystem picture
Anchoring on a single feature (e.g., organomegaly) rather than recognizing the required combination of core diagnostic criteria
reference.prognosis: With clone-directed therapy, many patients achieve meaningful and durable improvement in neuropathy and systemic features, and overall survival is generally more favorable than multiple myeloma. However, residual neurologic deficits are common, and relapse or progression can occur, warranting long-term surveillance of the monoclonal marker and VEGF level.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Plasma Cell Disorders chapter (POEMS syndrome/osteosclerotic myeloma section)
management: Direct treatment at the underlying clonal plasma cells rather than at the polyneuropathy itself
For isolated sclerotic bone lesions with limited marrow involvement, deliver radiotherapy to the localised lesion
For disseminated or marrow-based disease, use high-dose melphalan with autologous stem cell transplantation, or a lenalidomide- or bortezomib-based regimen with dexamethasone
Support the disabling neuropathy with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and mobility aids, and manage extravascular volume overload with diuretics
Track serum VEGF alongside neurological and systemic features to gauge treatment response and detect relapse
Coordinate haematology and neurology input, and consider thromboprophylaxis given the prothrombotic tendency

algorithms.title: Dispenzieri Diagnostic Criteria and Management Pathway for POEMS

steps.action: Patient presenting with progressive symmetrical peripheral polyradiculoneuropathy (demyelinating on EMG/NCS) PLUS monoclonal plasma cell proliferative disorder (almost always lambda light chain).
Screen for Castleman disease (lymph node biopsy), sclerotic bone lesions (whole-body low-dose CT or skeletal survey), and markedly elevated serum VEGF (> 3 to 4 times ULN).

Evaluate for Organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy), Extravascular volume overload (ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema), Endocrinopathy (hypogonadism, primary hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), and Skin changes (hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, glomeruloid hemangiomas, acrocyanosis).

steps.step: Lesion Staging & Radiation vs Systemic Therapy
steps.branch: Isolated Sclerotic Bone Lesion (<= 1 to 2 lesions)
steps.action: Radiation therapy (40 to 50 Gy) is curative for localized plasma cell lesion and results in dramatic hematologic and neurologic recovery.

steps.branch: Disseminated bone lesions or bone marrow involvement
steps.action: Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) conditioned with high-dose melphalan OR systemic lenalidomide + dexamethasone or bortezomib-based therapy. Monitor serum VEGF levels serially to assess treatment response.

algorithms.caption: Diagnosis requires both mandatory criteria, at least one other major criterion, and at least one minor criterion.
